Name: Terry Lambert
Question: What goes into making an OS to be Unix compliant certified?
Answer: A lot. I was the tech lead at Apple for making Mac OS X pass UNIX certification, and it was done to get Apple out of a $200M lawsuit filed by The Open Group, for use of the UNIX™ trademark in advertising. The lawsuit was filed because the owner of Mac OS X Server kept putting “UNIX” on the web site, and all other marketing collateral for the Server product. The options were: I was asked if I could lead a team to do #1. I said “Yes, under the condition that I could use the compliance project as a hammer to force other parts of the organization to make changes in their own code base, and that I could play it rather loose with commit rules regarding what it said in the bugs database for a given code change, and what the given code change actually did, in addition to what it said in the bugs database”. I was given the “go”. And so we ran the compliance test suite against the existing Mac OS source base, and it immediately errored out because of the header files. And Ed Moy and I made a two line change that moved a type definition from <stdio.h> to where it was supposed to be, instead. One line of change in <stdio.h>, and another in the file the type was actually supposed to be located in. And we ran the tests again, and one of the header file errors in the tests went away. So we did a “world build”, where everything that was in Mac OS X, including iTunes, got rebuilt. That — essentially, one line change — broke 152 (from memory; that number sticks up, but it might have only been 137) projects failed to build. Including iTunes. And so Ed and I went through, and fixed every single one of those projects to build with the change, or without the change. And we did another “world build”, and everything built. Yes, we had access to all of Apple’s source code, at that point in the game. And so we submitted high priority bug fixes to the projects, some of which downgraded the priority immediately, and some of which they simply fixed, since we had provided them with the patch already. And then the VP of engineering, Bertrand Serlet, re-escalated the priority on the ones which had been downgraded. And we committed the header file changes. At this point, we had to go back, and reassess the feasibility of the whole project. Ed and I felt it was doable in the timeframe, given the preconditions I had already placed on the project. Ed was willing to say anything directly. I said “yes”, putting my job on the line, were we given the “go”. It escalated up to Steve. We were given the “go”. It was, after all, saving Apple either $1 billion or $200 million plus revamping all of the Mac OS X Server marketing collateral, after all. We were promised 1/10th of the $200 million, or $20 million in stock, on completion. $10 million to me, $5 million to Ed, and $5 million to Karen Crippes, who was looking for a home in Mac OS X development, I knew was an amazing engineer, and who could be roped into being technical liaison and periodically kicking off the tests and complaining to Ed and I about things not passing. I got the $10 million, because it was going to be my job on the line, and potentially, my ability to work in industry at a high level, ever again, in the future. Also, the tech lead has to fix anything no one else fixes, or no one else can fix, because they are the DRI (Directly Responsible Individual). I also wasn’t just tech lead; I was de facto project manager. I wore a lot of hats. It was going to be long slog. I had estimated a year, for a team of 5 individuals: the three mousekateers (not a misspelling), two contractors — one for mostly user space code; that was Len Lattanzi, and one for full time test automation and bug filing, Jaime Delgadillo, who also contributed patches, where possible. We had two more temporary contractors; one for tools compliance, and one for the man pages. And then anyone we could rope in from elsewhere in Apple, on a case by case basis, for a short term. This was mostly to make sure they were invested in the project; we didn’t actually need them to write code. Our first red letter day was when all the header files passed testing, so that the other tests in the test suite would start running. We actually committed all the header file changes to the rest of Mac OS X, by that time. The headers were standards compliant By the time Tiger shipped. This broke the heck out of Code Warrior. I fully intended to fix that, but was never given the opportunity, and Code Warrior was more or less collateral damage. But it was a red letter day when the header files passed testing, and we celebrated by going out to IL6 — the informal name for the BJ’s restaurant, just off the Apple campus. As far as the rest of Apple was concerned, we had just closed the “Fix Header Files” bug, which encompassed a lot of other bugs that were for individual header files. We had spend about 3 months doing this. I had promised a year. How was I going to hit the one year estimate? I knew going in that forcing the header file changes — and the project changes associated with them — would be the biggest individual part of the project. Once we could run the other tests, there was a lot of “low hanging fruit” to fix in other areas. That took about two months, playing fast and loose with the commit rules, and we made short work of them. Ed did most of the libSystem — libc + other system libraries, rolled into one — with assistance from me inmoving things out of the namespace; this is why there are header files in /usr/include/sys that begin with “_”, for example. While waiting on submissions, you could do other work in parallel, and we did. After the low hanging fruit, there was a lot of other work, like rewriting the signal system in the kernel, which was not that low hanging. By this time, we had roped in Umesh (I won’t give his last name), because he didn’t want us touching his pthreads code, and he wanted to make changes there anyway, and having the project as a means of hammering through those changes pleased him greatly. We bought begrudging buy-in from Mike Smith (yes, *that* Mike Smith) by having him rewrite the file locking code. I’m the one who pushed it out of individual filesystems, and into the layer above, so that it was one common code implementation. But Mike was the one who made it work. We finally bought Joe Sokol off by asking questions about the trap path, and surrounding the signals system stack frame saves. Of these, however, it was Umesh who was most helpful in meeting our deadline. Eventually, we had everything working and passing the tests. We were ready to pull the trigger. And then they pulled in the Intel code changes, and crapped all over everything, because we were told to wait two weeks. It was a mess. And so I spent a three day bender, reintegrating all our patches on the conformance branch into post-Intel kernel code. By this time, I knew pretty much every one of the 13 million lines of kernel code in the Mac OS X kernel. And we were back to passing the tests. And then we were told we could not integrate for Tiger. That we would miss our self-imposed deadline. Because it was “too much change at once, with the Intel changes”. Tiger dragged on for another 6 months before release, with week-for-week slips. This was because of Intel-specific bugs — not in the kernel. We could have, in other words, easily shipped in Tiger. And hit our self-imposed deadline. If I were asked to do the same thing for Linux, it likely would take five years, and two dozen people. Linux is pretty balkanize, has a lot of kingdom building, and you have to pee on everything to make it smell like Linux. I could do the same in FreeBSD in about a year and a half, with a dozen co-conspirators to run the changes through. A lot of the work would happen in the “ports” tree. All told, probably 4% of the 6% of the Max OS X kernel that I wrote? It came from the UNIX conformance changes. IT came from committing massive signals changes, and attributing them to a simple signal bug resulting in a kernel crash, in the “Radar” bugs database. A lot of the things Ed did to libc header files, and libc itself, had similar “fibs” in Radar. We had a lot of gratitude in the Open Source community — particular for our fixes to make bash pass the tests. You have absolutely no idea how much Apple contributed to the Open Source community, as part of this project, because it was a secret project — at least to people outside Apple — so we didn’t advertise the fact. But I expect we contributed about two million lines of code, to hundreds of Open Source projects, over the course of that year. A lot of gratitude — but it wasn’t collective, and so Apple was still faulted for “using Open Source code, but never contributing back”. We fixed at least 15 major gcc bugs, for example. You have no idea. So overall? It’s a pretty big project to get compliance. And that before all the things that Karen did, on the self-certification, contracts, getting test exception based on existing exception for OSF/1 Mach, and so on. It was, indeed, a long slog.

Question: When I search online to troubleshoot software problems, the “solutions” I find usually have commands that aren’t in any of my drop-down menus. What am I not seeing here?
Answer: Whenever you get into an abnormal situation with software, there are no canned answers to fix the issue, and therefore there is no canned menu item which can be used to implement a canned answer. Instead, you end up having to use specific tools, frequently command line command tools, but also potentially others, to resolve the problem. The commands you need are likely there, but you need to open a terminal window to get at them (or for Windows, a command/power shell/other command line tool). It may also be necessary to have developer tools installed on the system, in order to have some of these commands available at all in this first place; for example, on macOS/Mac OS X, it’s often necessary to have the XCode installed, with the optional command line tools, installed. For complex issues, this means that you have to dismount the disk drive/persistent storage from the device, and actually use another machine to do the work. Consider this analogy… Even if you are a “shade tree mechanic”, working on a car from about the 1980’s onward will not really be an option for you, unless you have extremely sophisticated tools, such as those required to diagnose a faulty engine control computer. “No User Serviceable Parts Inside”. Human bodies are actually quite similar, and it takes a lot of experience as a “biohacker” to fix certain sophisticated problems,on a case-by-case basis. “No User Serviceable Parts Inside”. So for some problems — especially intentionally caused problems, or problems cause as a side effect of an intentional effect. Call it “malware”, for computers, or “recreational drug use”, for human bodies, or “street racing”, for cars; in the limit, it often requires an expert to undo something which has gone wrong, and resulted in a subsequent cascade failure. If you can’t understand the suggested fix, then get someone who knows what they are doing to help you, in other words.

So you don’t get it as reference code,unless you are talking about the use of a specific PI middleware library API, which means you endorse a specific product capable of running on all your platforms. Note that any such middleware layer will damage performance on all platforms, unless it’s made to look exactly like one of the platforms native networking APIs, at which point it will be fast on that one platform, and suck everywhere else.

Question: How does the performance and security of open source Darwin compare to mainstream Linux, BSD, and other Unix systems?
Answer: Darwin is essentially macOS, without the proprietary optimizations licensed from other sources, and sits as an integrated BSD “Single Server” on top of OSF/Mach. There are certain aspects of this arrangement which lead to lower performance — the math libraries, especially, are lower performance than the licensed libraries you can’t have. The additional boundary layering can also cost performance. As can certain features, such as membership of a given user credential or filesystem or other credentialed object in an essentially unlimited number of groups. However, Darwin is extremely secure, much more than Linux or BSD, because of the way that the user/kernel boundary crossing credential enforcement is handled. Note: I wrote almost all of that code But realize that there are also things about Darwin that are not covered via the same security capabilities in specialty versions of BSD or Linux, such as seLinux, or seBSD — particularly now that the MACF framework and loading of kernel modules in macOS has been deprecated. So, for example, there are a number of NSA security modules you can no longer load into macOS, and therefore Darwin, that you can load in those Linux and BSD variants, such as FLASK and TE: You should really get out more, and read more security related CS research papers. You also need to be aware that instead of dealing with Darwin, you can simply download the macOS source code from Apple, and use that instead. Most people don’t use Darwin directly because of this. But if you want a particular example, if you look at the SUGID code in Darwin/macOS, abd compare it with that in Linux and BSD variants, you will likely see a group membership hole you could drive a truck through, as a security bug in both of them. Particularly as regards “exclusion groups”, which is about as big a hint as I am willing to get. You will also see in the group enforcement code a reversal of the order of group/world checking, which is a performance enhancement on which I have a pending patent of mine, assigned to Apple.

These days, there’s an overreliance on SIGINT. This is including, but not limited to, cryptography, which is code breaking. But bugs, hidden cameras, old fashioned telephone taps, parabolic microphones, the wearing of wires by sources or participants, traffic analysis and so on. It can also include circumstantial evidence, such as determining someone’s cell phone was in proximity to a crime, without needing to know the contents of a conversation, either via Stingray style systems, or cell tower triangulation (though this is easily spoofed, which is what makes it circumstantial). An overreliance on SIGINT is why the FBI and DOJ are frequently requesting ”back doors” in cryptographic systems, so that they don’t actually have to do police work, and collect information another way. Al Capone was brought don not for his criminal acts; in the end it was tax evasion that landed him in prison. I think that as technology advances, much of what it takes to commit crimes, particularly non-conesnual crimes, will remain the same as it has always been: means,motive, and opportunity. I think a lot of technologically enabled crimes are never prosecuted, in large part because they are international, and no one bothers to put in the effort to prosecute them, or because they are interstate, and the viCtims always take the crimes to their local law enforcement, instead of the correct agency. The correct agency for interstate is the FBI, and they are frequently uninterested in what are considered “petty crimes” — for example, wire fraud, where a lot of people are defrauded,but the fraud amounts are kept relatively small. For example, there is a credit card fraud ring operating in the San Francisco Bay Area by obtaining records for self storage unit companies, through poor cybersecurity protocols on the part of those companies. The companies themselves often have proper partitioning of the billing systems, but often also keep the last 4 digits of the billing credit card on file with the other information in the customer record, in order to issue billing statements. Then they call someone up, pretext as the storage unit, and “verify” their identity through the information they know, and through the last 4 digits of the credit card. Then claim the last payment did not go through, and get full card information from the person they call, in order to make small charges using the card, and then sell the card onward to card theft rings who operate as aggregators of stolen card information. All the charges are kept below the “interest threshold”, both for police agencies, such as the FBI, and often low enough that the credit card fraud departments are also not interested in following up. The “test charge” is often a temporary hold of a small amount, which does not register as a charge at all, or is a small amount through a front company. Said companies are usually located in urban areas in Florida. There is also a lot of non-prosecution of scam and SPAM calling, which is usually under the jurisdiction of the FTC. This is rarely prosecuted, either under federal law, or under state law; for example, unsolicited phone calls, in California, carry a penalty per call that, in bulk, they would be worth prosecuting, but are never prosecuted. Many of these are interstate or international calls,placing them directly under the purview of the FBI, in terms of investigation, but would require a state level prosecution, and thus require interagency cooperation, separating the investigation from the prosecution across jurisdictional lines. Such crimes are rarely prosecuted. Similarly, the federal government actively assists in many of these frauds, particularly international frauds perpetrated using robocalling. The frauds are perpetrated on the basis of international VOIP calling from call centers in India, and elsewhere. Here is an example that too three years to bust: (this is on a Youtube channel called “Scammer Payback”). Again, we find that the major problem is a jurisdictional boundary. In this case, the boundary in question is the FCC tariffs on what are called common carriers, and what a common carrier is and is not allowed to do, and the regulation of interstate commerce by the Interstate Commerce Commission, and the regulation of international commerce via the U.S. State Department. This intersects at FCC tariffs because the FCC regulations define what is and is not disqualifying behaviour by a common carrier. Because of this, it’s impossible to, for example, have common carriers block international VOIP calls, even if requested by the customer. In fact, common carriers are paid on the basis of call termination, which means a number of counterintuitive things: In fact, the combination of #5 and #6 are what are used for SWATting. This is where you call a non-emergency services number, and get transferred to an emergency services number, or it is otherwise treated as an emergency services call, so that there is no out of band ANI (Automatic Number Identification) information for the real caller. And then you attempt murder by police proxy, by claiming a hostage situation, shots fired, and so on, which the Call ID (spoofed) backs up as legitimately coming from a neighbor., in order to elicit a SWAT response. And obviously, since “the neighbor” is kept on the line, there is no outbound call made to the neighbor to verify, and even sere such a call made, very few legitimate callers would drop the police call, having been ordered to stay on the line, to answer “another call coming in”. So the call is taken at face value, and attempted murder by police proxy ensues. There is a very obvious impedance mismatch here, in the systems design, which can be abused, is abused — often by one teenage gamer against another —and has resulted in tragic deaths, in the past. All because the FCC regulations will not change. Personally, I think most of these issues are due to a lack of formal police work, and bad systems engineering, and bad laws. This isn’t the fault of the FBI, but so long as the FBI is lobbying for the wrong thing as their top priority — back doors for cryptosystems — instead of addressing real systems and procedural deficiencies— they are not lobbying for the right things, the problems will persist. One very obvious thing is… why, when I transfer a call from a non-emergency number, to an emergency services number, is ANI information for the orginal caller not available to emergency services? Why can a gamer kid in Canada pretend to be a next door neighbor in the U.S., and get a SWAT unit out to someone’s house? Until the obvious systems problems are addressed, I really don’t see the other issues as important, relatively speaking. And by the way? Try doing some real police work, and engaging in more HUMINT, and less SIGINT, in the future. Several flight schools called in the students who were interested in learning to fly, but not how to land, prior to the 9/11 attacks, and nothing was done about that HUMINT, which was available before the fact, actionable, but not acted upon. Question: My WiFi is not connecting after changing my IMEI address. What can I do to fix it?

Your WiFi controller has a MAC address, and no one really cares what the MAC address is, ever, because ARP can map the MAC address to the assigned IP address in the ARP table,and then everything is by IP address, unless it’s a link.local or other non-routable link. Question: Why was ATT broken up by anti-trust actions while much larger companies like Apple, Amazon, and Google have not?

Instead, Microsoft settled the case with the Department of Justice in 2001 by agreeing to make it easier for competitors to integrate their software with Windows. National security interests were also cited, in camera, which apparently persuaded the 5th Circuit to get out of the breakup by agreeing to something they should have been doing in the first place. So: Not a monopoly. AMAZON: Amazon has a natural monopoly, unless you want to purchase through Ali, Ali Express, Temu, or another Chinese company. LAtely, DHGate is gaining ground, but it’s got a UI lifted straight off Amazon and mated with TEMU, to create this weird thing that is, well, DHGate. What cause Amazon’s natural monopoly? Sales tax. Specifically, Amazon agreed to collect sales tax on behalf of sales, to appease states that wanted to collect sales tax, and couldn’t, because people are mostly unwilling to pay a “use tax” on things purchased out of state, and sent mail-order. Mostly, California is pissy about this tax being paid. By agreeing to pay sales tax, it’s almost impossible to compete woith Amazon, because it’s nearly impossible for a small Internet store to collect the proper tax, or even know who to pay it out to. Here’s a company that tries, with varying degrees of success, to sell you services, if you are a small web site: The first sentence from the quote from their site is the big point: In the U.S., there are over 13,000 sales and use tax jurisdictions. Each of these jurisdictions will have multiple tax rates, which may also change frequently depending on economic circumstances. With so much to keep track of, many international businesses trading in the United States for the first time end up struggling with U.S. tax compliance. Other people can’t compete with Amazon, and Amazon has a natural monopoly, because they agreed to do something for government, which government could not do for themselves. And which represents a massive barrier to entry for any company not also as large as Amazon, who wishes to compete, even in a half-assed way, with Amazon. So other than keeping people out of their market — and it’s probably a violation of the Sherman Antitrust Acts for natural monopolies to exist, but what can you do about it? — they really haven’t been abusive about it. And the Amazon case would go away, if everyone could just give a shipping address and a sales amount, and the system gives them the tax owed,m and where to send it, and they just send it. So breaking up Amazon would break a lot of state revenue collection models, which are best described as “make the actual collection of the tax someone else’s problem”. Question: If I flash Kali Linux to a USB drive from my Windows laptop (using an ONN drive), can I boot from the USB drive on my MacBook Air?
Answer: Is it a MacBook Air Kali image? My understanding is that Linux still calls ExitBootServices(), which means that it wants another <128K or so of memory back, from the boot process. You can’t call ExitBootServices() on a MacBook Air; it uses the Intel reference UEFI implementation, which has an attribute bug on a number of pages which are required to be maintained after the call, but they are in fact discarded, and a number of other UEFI calls, if made subsequently, will catastrophically fail (the system just reboots, instead of booting Linux). Since many, many people’s UEFI’s have this same bug, being derived from the Intel Reference Implementation, you will find Linux similarly will not UEFI boot on those platforms, either, You can call it a UEFI bug, but since commenting out the call in the Linux source code works around the problem on all platforms, and loses you less than 128K, the only reason for Linux to be stubborn about this is that there are people who want to feel important. If you, on the other hand, comment out the call, and build your own Kali Linux distribution, everything will just work.

Question: What specific problem does the SaaS solution solve?
Answer: Let me explain. Some companies want an ongoing revenue stream. If they sell you the software once, they do not have an ongoing revenue stream. You could take it to Mars with you, where Internet access would be impossible, without CoLo facilities also located on Mars. But they would not get ongoing revenue; they would only be paid one time. By selling you instead use of the software, not the software itself, they get paid for your ability to use it, as an ongoing revenue stream. Hence Microsoft Office 365. Microsoft Office 365 solves the problem of an ongoing revenue stream for Microsoft, so that they don’t have to innovate, or provide new products, but can instead just kick back and collect money every month, with a practical guarantee of future income, which they can borrow against, and spend on other things unrelated to actually providing Office, or to making Office better. Additionally, they can sell you security services, which would not be necessary, were you not accessing it over the Internet, but instead running it locally, and storage services, which would not be necessary, if the data resided on your hard drive. So for $359.64/year, you get a product which would have had a one time cost of $359.64, but could be used for decades, without paying additional money to Microsoft. So the problem it solves is the “how does a company continue to milk a customer for money, after it has already sold something?” problem. Question: On the government telephone system network, how are state long distance and local calls billed and charged as opposed to commercial phone calls?
Answer: I assume you are aware that it has been between 30 and 50 years since trunking and circuit switching for phone calls was a common thing. Today, phone calls occur over virtual circuits,over a packet switch network,much of which is implemented on top of ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Method). The simple answer as to how things are billed is that billing happens based on the particular tariff being applied to the particular call. The tariffs, in turn, are established by negotiations between the telephone carriers, and the locla PUC (Public Utilities Commission). And then you are billed on “events” covered by the tariff in question. This usually includes whether or not the service is metered rate, whether or not “long distance” — meaningless to the packet WATS lines, payphones, etc.. There is usualy a cost for “call setup”, “call teardown”, and then per minute charges, if you are under a metered rate tariff. As part of call setup, the telephone company gets paid for “call completion”, even if you never talk to the human you are calling (what used to be referred to as a “person to person” call). So the phone company gets paid if: It’s in their financial best interest to let SPAM/scam calls reach you. That,plus it avoids them losing common carrier status, as a result of specific FCC regulations to allow political and 501(c)(3) charities to make unsolicited phone calls, with no preexisting business relationship. So… counter question… What tariff(s) apply to the calling plan you are curently using? This will allow you to accurately predict what a given call will or will not cost you.
